title: Design restaurants near me
dek: Open Zotato in Koramangala at 8 pm and the home screen lists restaurants that deliver to you, nearest and best first, in a blink. Find those few hundred among 3 lakh restaurants, thousands of times a second, while kitchens switch on and off all evening.

items: All 3 lakh restaurants fit in about 300 MB, so the data isn't the problem. The problem is answering "what's near this point?" 6,000 times a second.
A normal index can't do it: an index on latitude alone returns a strip across the whole country. You need a geo index that keeps nearby places together.
Geohash cuts the map into named cells; places close together share a prefix. Look up your cell and its 8 neighbours, never just your own.
"Near me" for delivery means "delivers to me". Keep a list per cell of the restaurants that serve it, and check open or busy at query time.
Many people in one area ask the same question at dinner: cache each cell's candidates for a minute or so.
Given the customer's location, list restaurants that deliver there, open right now.
Sort by distance, rating or delivery time, and filter by cuisine, veg only, or rating 4+.
Scroll through results page by page without seeing the same restaurant twice.
Restaurants can change their own status: open, busy (taking fewer orders) or closed.
Out of scope here: search by dish name, personal ranking, and how the delivery time is worked out (that's dispatch).

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: Results in under 200 ms for nearly every request
A closed kitchen disappears within a minute; a new restaurant shows within an hour
The home screen always loads; slightly old results beat an error
3 lakh restaurants, 2 crore people opening the app each day

items: Data: 3 lakh restaurants × about 1 KB (location, cuisines, rating, zone) is 300 MB. It fits in memory on one server, so every server can hold a full copy.
Reads: 2 crore people × 5 home-screen loads is 10 crore a day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200 a second, about 6,000 at the dinner peak. Dinner packs most of the day's opens into a few hours.
Writes: locations almost never change. Status does: 3 lakh restaurants × about 10 changes a day is 30 lakh a day, about 35 a second.
So this is read-heavy by a wide margin, and small enough to copy everywhere. The design follows from that.
Restaurant: `id`, `name`, `lat`, `lng`, `cuisines`, `veg_only`, `rating`, `zone` (where it delivers).
Status: `restaurant_id`, `state` (open, busy, closed), `until`.
Cell: a geohash, and the list of restaurants that deliver into it.

body.label: API
body.say: Two calls. The customer app asks for nearby restaurants with its latitude and longitude, a sort order, filters and a cursor, and gets a page of restaurants with distance, rating and delivery time, plus a cursor for the next page. The restaurant app sets its status to open, busy or closed, optionally until a time.

body.cap: The nearby service turns the customer's location into a cell, reads which restaurants deliver into that cell from an in-memory geo index, drops the ones that are closed or busy, adds names and ratings from a cache, ranks them and returns the first 20.

body.x: The nearby service is stateless and keeps the whole geo index in memory, so adding servers adds capacity. The restaurant database stays the source of truth; every change flows from it to the index through a change stream, and status lives in Redis because it changes all evening.

body.name: First try
body.what: Store `lat` and `lng` with an index on each, and ask for rows where both fall inside a box around the customer.
body.use: Works with any database and is easy to explain.
body.avoid: The database usually uses one index well. `lat BETWEEN …` alone matches a strip across the whole country, and every row in it is then checked for longitude.
body.ex: A box around Koramangala matches every restaurant at that latitude, from Mangaluru to Chennai.
body.like: Looking for your neighbours by asking everyone born in the same year.

body.name: Better
body.what: Interleave the bits of latitude and longitude into one short string. Each extra character makes the cell smaller, and places close together share a prefix, so a normal index on the string finds them.
body.use: One index, prefix lookups, works in any database or in Redis (which uses the same idea for its geo commands).
body.avoid: Two places a few metres apart can sit either side of a cell border and share no prefix. Always search your cell and the 8 around it.
body.ex: 5-character cells are roughly 5 km a side; 6-character cells are about 1.2 × 0.6 km.
body.like: PIN codes: neighbours usually share the first digits, but the house across a district border doesn't.

body.name: Best
body.kind: CELLS THAT SPLIT WHERE IT'S BUSY
body.what: A quadtree starts with the whole map as one cell and splits any cell holding more than, say, 100 restaurants into four, again and again.
body.use: Dense areas get small cells and empty areas big ones, so every lookup touches about the same number of restaurants.
body.avoid: It lives in memory and must be rebuilt or updated as restaurants are added. In an interview, say that databases' built-in geo indexes (PostGIS, MongoDB's 2dsphere) already do this kind of work.
body.ex: Koramangala ends up in cells a few hundred metres wide; a stretch of highway in Rajasthan is one cell tens of kilometres wide.
body.like: A city map with an inset for the crowded old town.

body.cap: The customer is near the edge of their cell. Biryani Zone is 300 m away but in the next cell, so searching one cell misses it. Searching the 3 × 3 block finds it. With cells at least as wide as the search radius, the block always covers the circle.

body.x: A restaurant 2 km away across Silk Board may not deliver to you, while one 6 km away on a straight road does. Each restaurant has its own delivery zone, which Zotato shrinks when it rains hard or riders are short. So the question isn't "who is within 5 km" but "whose zone contains this point".

items: Turn it around: for every small cell, keep the list of restaurants whose zone covers it. A lookup is then one read by cell id. A cell goes on a restaurant's list if its zone touches the cell at all; check the exact point against the zone afterwards. That's why one cell is enough here, while a radius search needs all nine.
Rebuild a restaurant's cells when its zone changes. That's a few hundred cells, a handful of times a day, which is cheap.
Check status after the lookup, from Redis. Busy and closed change every few minutes, so they never go into the index itself.

Thousands of people in the same few cells ask the same question at once. Cache the cell's candidates (with ratings) for 30 to 60 seconds; most home screens become a cache read. Sort by distance per request; 200 items is cheap.
Apply status after the cache, so a kitchen that just closed disappears at once even when the cached list still has it.
Every nearby server has the full index in memory. Add servers for more reads; no sharding is needed at 300 MB.
If the index or Redis is slow, show the last cached list for the cell. A slightly old home screen is better than an empty one.
Take the 200 or so restaurants in the cells, sort by the chosen order, and return 20 at a time.
Straight-line distance is fine for sorting candidates; show delivery time from the dispatch service only for the page on screen.
Results change between pages as kitchens open and close. Keep the candidate list for a few minutes behind the cursor, so the second page carries on from the first without repeats.
Junior / mid: why a plain index on latitude and longitude fails, one geo index (geohash is fine), checking neighbouring cells, and a cache.
Senior: the numbers (300 MB, 6,000 reads a second) leading to an in-memory index on every server, delivery zones rather than radius, status kept apart from the index.
Lead: freshness through a change stream, caching per cell with status applied afterwards, stable pages, and what the home screen shows when parts of this are down.
"What if nothing is open within reach?" Say so and suggest scheduling for later, rather than silently showing restaurants that can't deliver.
"The customer is moving, say in an auto." Ask for results again only when they move into a new cell, not on every location update.
"Restaurants in 800 cities, not one?" Still 300 MB in total, so every server keeps all of it. Split by city only if the data grows a lot, for example with dish-level search.
"How is distance worked out?" The haversine formula gives straight-line distance on a sphere. Road distance comes from the maps or dispatch service, and only for the few results on screen.
"How do you test it?" Seed known points near cell borders and on both sides of a zone boundary, and check that the right restaurants come back.

body.x: "The menu everyone reads" is the same shape as the 8 pm home screen: a flood of identical reads. Put a cache in front and watch the database calm down.

practice.brief: Each test sends home-screen loads ("what's near me, open now"). Each load makes one lookup; restaurant data changes rarely, so a cache answers 95% of lookups. Your Clients' own rate is ignored.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 2,000 home-screen loads a second at 3 pm.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of home screens succeed

tests.name: The dinner peak
tests.desc: 6,000 loads a second at 8:30 pm. Results must come back fast.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of home screens succeed

tests.name: The match ends
tests.desc: At 8 pm the cricket final ends and everyone opens Zotato at once: 15,000 loads a second for 15 minutes.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of home screens succeed

tests.name: A server group dies
tests.desc: At the peak (6,000 a second) the busiest group of servers crashes; it is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of home screens still succeed

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the busiest database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

checks.label: At least 99.8% of home screens still succeed
Every database has a standby in another zone (Multi-AZ)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (2,000 a second). Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails, like a memory limit.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of home screens succeed

fr.label: List restaurants near my location that deliver to me

est.label: Home-screen loads a second at peak
est.how: 2 crore people × 5 loads ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,200 a second; dinner packs it ~5×

est.label: Size of all restaurant data
est.how: 3 lakh × ~1 KB: small enough for every server to keep a copy

hints.x: What does the home screen show, and what can a restaurant change about itself during dinner?
Work out the size of all restaurant data. If it is a few hundred MB, where can it live?
One read with a location, sort, filters and a cursor; one write for a restaurant's status.
Reads outnumber writes about 200 to 1, and the data is tiny. Answer reads from memory, not the database.
Put a Cache in front of the database: at 95% hits, 6,000 loads a second become 300 database queries.
When the match ends, traffic jumps 2.5× in a minute. Have the servers for it before 8 pm: autoscaling needs 4 minutes.
Two server groups and a Multi-AZ database keep the home screen up when something dies.

wrong.name: No cache
wrong.why: Every read goes to the database, which can't take the peak.

wrong.name: One server group
wrong.why: When it crashes, nothing answers for 5 minutes.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: A crash keeps it down for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Passes the load but costs far more than the traffic needs.
